title: Building on the Moon
objective: After this level you can explain plans for bases on the Moon.
summary: The Moon has no shielding air and wild temperature swings. A pressurized habitat is mainly in tension. ESA's 2013 study proposed a printed regolith catenary dome over an inflatable.

cards.headline: On the Moon, the biggest push on a building comes from inside it.
cards.body: A Moon base has to hold Earth-level air pressure where there's no atmosphere outside. That outward push is several orders of magnitude bigger than the gravity and weather loads on buildings on Earth. It turns Chapter 1's rules inside out.

cards.headline: A tough building site
cards.body: The Moon has only a very thin atmosphere, so nothing blocks the Sun's radiation or incoming meteoroids. In full sunlight its surface reaches about 127 °C; in darkness it drops to about -173 °C. That's a swing of about 300 degrees between sunlight and shadow. Gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, so everything weighs less, but that's the only easy part.

cards.headline: The inside-out building
cards.body: On Earth, gravity squeezes buildings: Level 2's compression. A pressurized Moon habitat is mainly in tension instead, its walls pushed outward and stretched by the air inside. Here's an analogy: a balloon's skin, pulled tight by the air it holds. To protect it, engineers suggest a thick outer layer of regolith, the Moon's loose, broken soil and rock, to dampen temperature swings and shield against radiation.

cards.fact: In 2013, ESA tested printing a Moon base from Moon soil.
cards.context: ESA and partners including the architects Foster + Partners studied whether a 3D printer could build a lunar base from regolith. The design: an inflatable, pressurized dome to shelter astronauts, covered by a robot-printed regolith shell. The shell was a weight-bearing catenary dome with hollow, closed cells like bird bones. A catenary is a hanging chain's curve: flip it and you get Level 10's arch. The team printed a 1.5-tonne demonstration block. It was a study, not a base.

mascot.line: Hooke's hanging chain, from 1675 all the way to the Moon. Good ideas travel well.

cards.headline: Moon building: mapped
learned: Air pressure pushes out, so habitats are mainly in tension
Regolith cover could shield and steady temperatures
ESA, 2013: printed regolith catenary dome over an inflatable

questions.prompt: In ESA's 2013 lunar base study, what would the robot printer build the shell from?

options.label: Concrete shipped up from Earth
options.rationale: The study's printer used regolith, found on the Moon.

options.label: Regolith, the Moon's loose soil and rock
Blocks of ice cut from craters
options.rationale: The shell was printed from regolith.

options.label: Steel panels bolted together
options.rationale: The shell was printed, not bolted.

questions.explanation: ESA and Foster + Partners studied printing a regolith shell over an inflatable dome.

questions.prompt: Why is a pressurized Moon habitat mainly in tension, unlike a building on Earth?

options.label: Moon gravity pulls it upward
options.rationale: Gravity still pulls down, just more weakly.

options.label: Meteoroids pull on its roof
options.rationale: Impacts don't pull; the air inside pushes.

options.label: Its walls are made of stretched rope
options.rationale: The tension comes from air pressure, not the material.

options.label: Air inside pushes out, with almost none outside

questions.explanation: With almost no atmosphere outside, the air inside pushes the walls outward and stretches them: tension.

questions.prompt: Foster + Partners shaped ESA's printed lunar shell as a catenary dome. Which Level 10 idea does that shape use?

options.label: A dome's lower rings stretch like barrel hoops
A beam is squeezed on top, stretched below
A hanging chain, flipped, stands as an arch
A frame carries floors so walls can be glass

questions.explanation: A catenary is a hanging chain's curve; Hooke showed that, turned upside down, it stands as an arch in compression.
